subjects.name: Rick Walker
subjects.profile: Rick Walker — K-8 Teacher,Former Line cook

sources.name: Patricia Nolan
sources.quote: When I walk past the school now, I see the same kids I always saw — the ones who show up early to help the janitor, the ones who pass notes in the back, the ones who ask the question that stops the whole lesson because they actually want to know. The index doesn't see any of that. It sees a number. But I've watched those kids for thirty years, and I know the difference between a kid who can't learn and a kid who hasn't been given a reason to yet. That 6.3 — it doesn't tell you about the girl who reads to her little brother every night because their mom works late, or the boy who fixes the classroom door hinge because he notices it's loose. Those kids are there, all 314 of them, and they're not flat numbers. They're just waiting for someone to see them the way I got to see them.

sources.name: Jun Leu
sources.quote: A typical day is pretty normal, I guess. I walk to school, sit through classes, eat lunch with my friends, try to pay attention when the teacher's talking. Some days are boring, some days are fun. I don't really think about numbers or ratings or whatever. I just know my teachers show up and try, and most kids are just trying to get through the day like anywhere else. I wish people outside the neighborhood wouldn't judge our school just by some score. We're not broken or anything. We're just a school. The people here care about us, and we're doing fine.

sources.name: Rick Walker
sources.quote: I see that 6.3 and I think about what it means to teach in a place that isn't growing. When the district puts money and attention where the numbers are moving, a flat school just... sits there. Those 314 kids and their teachers aren't a statistic to me — they're showing up every day doing the work with less, and nobody's knocking on their door asking what they need.

excludedLeads.text: A retired teacher in Temescal might say the school's problems are about funding — $11,500 per student versus Rockridge's $15,000 — but that's a hunch until she says it.
Students might describe the gap between what the school offers and what they need for college, but I won't know until I ask.
The district's growth — 5,201 employees, up 7.37% — might not be reaching Temescal's classrooms, but that's an interpretation, not a fact on the table.
